subject: lion
pitch: A proud old lion resting with his head held high. A huge shaggy mane fading from golden blond at the face to dark chocolate at the edges, a tawny body with a pale cream belly and muzzle, amber eyes, a broad black nose, a scar across one eyebrow, big padded paws and a long tail ending in a dark tuft.
reasoning:
I'm planning the structure of a TypeScript module that builds a lion using the SDK, reviewing the key joint, chain, and sweep APIs I'll need to get the proportions and anatomy correct.

I'll export a default function returning b.root along with a meta object, and I'm thinking through the pose — likely a resting or seated lion with its head held high to match the brief.

For the actual geometry, I'm planning a sphinx-style pose: hindquarters on the ground, front legs extended forward, chest raised, head lifted, with body dimensions scaled to roughly real lion proportions. I'll build it from sweeps and chains for the body and legs, a tail sweep, and a mane assembled from cards or spikes around the head, possibly painted with a gradient for shading.

I'm figuring out how to paint the mane with a color gradient fading by distance from the face center, checking that the mix/paint utilities I need are exported correctly without naming conflicts.

For the mane geometry itself, I'm considering a lathe-based shell around the head and neck — using a surface of revolution with a profile radius along the head's axis, shaped like a flattened ring or torus.

Actually, switching approach: using many card elements arranged radially around the head, each textured with an SVG fur-tuft shape and tinted with a gradient paint from face to edge, since cards accept a Paint color and a texture parameter. I'd generate the SVG tuft as a tapered blade path to use as the card texture.

Cards placed on the ring frames use the outward direction as their facing axis, so lean 0 makes mane tufts stand straight out from the head, radiating outward with a slight backward bend for flow. I'm working through how the ring-around-line setup orients each item perpendicular to the central forward-facing axis.

I'm considering using tilt to lean mane strands backward away from the face, but worrying a full 360-degree ring would place cards over the face itself, so I may need to restrict the ring to an angular range that excludes the front and only covers the back and sides of the head.

I realize the ring should sit slightly behind the head center so the mane frames the cheeks while leaving the face front exposed, with radius larger than the head's half-width so cards sit outside it. Rather than keep refining this abstractly, I should just lock down concrete coordinates: lion facing +Z, roughly 1.3m tall at the head in a resting sphinx pose, starting from ground level and building up the hips and body from there.

Now I'm placing the pose in detail—hips, chest, shoulders, and head positions for a sphinx stance with forelegs extended, then haunches and rear paws for the sitting hindquarters, and sketching a spine curve connecting hip to shoulder as the backbone for the body's sweep geometry.

Setting up the spine chain and radius function...

Thinking about the names array length relative to spans count: with 3 spans I need 3 or 4 names, so using ['hip','waist','chest'] with 3 joints and no tip works fine.

I need a root joint before the chain since the first joint's parent defaults by searching nearest built joints — so I'll create a 'pelvis' root joint first at roughly (0, 0.45, -0.55) with direction [0,0,1], then build the spine chain from there.

Actually simplifying: make the root joint 'body' with no parent, then set the spine chain's parent explicitly to 'body' rather than relying on auto-nearest. For the head, instead of another full catmull chain, I'll place a single 'head' joint and build a short neck chain from the chest position up to the head base using a catmull path.

Simplifying by naming the neck chain's tip joint 'head' directly rather than adding a separate head joint afterward, then continuing on to define the jaw joint.

Still defining head geometry...

For the mane gradient I'm blending blond near the face to chocolate at the edges based on each card's root distance from a face point in front of the head — cards near the front stay blond while those toward the back darken, giving a natural fade across the mane.

Now I'm figuring out the ring placement for the mane cards: positioning a frame just in front of the head joint, oriented to face forward, so the ring of cards wraps around correctly and the weight/bone binding flows through to each card's root.

Tuning the mane proportions now — radius around 0.2 with cards sized roughly 0.22 long by 0.12 wide, pointing radially outward with no lean but a back-leaning bend around 40 degrees to give it flow.

For the card texture, I'm designing a simple tapered tuft shape as an SVG path, white-filled so it can be tinted via vertex colors from the paint system rather than a fixed hue. I need to make sure the textured material handles alpha correctly so the tuft shape reads cleanly against the background.

For the mane gradient, I'm defining a smoothstep-based blend between blond and chocolate tones based on distance from a face reference point, making sure the mix order gives blond near the face and chocolate farther away.

Working through the geometry now, checking the actual distances from the various card positions to the face center—most come out around 0.27-0.28, which with my chosen threshold range would push the mane mostly dark. I should widen the gradient range so more blond shows through near the face.

I'm also thinking about the body coloring: tawny back fading to cream belly, using a countershade function with a negative level and soft blend so the sweep between colors feels natural rather than abrupt.

Writing body paint logic...

Now I'm planning the front leg geometry for the sphinx pose — defining joint positions from shoulder to elbow, wrist, and paw toe, then building the chain structure to connect them.

The exact parent position doesn't matter much since it's just determining the transform origin. For the leg sweep, I'm tapering the radius from upper arm down to wrist, then adding a padded paw as a separate sphere scaled flatter and wider at the foot position, keeping it tawny-colored with room for optional dark claws.

Now I'm working out the hind leg structure for a sitting pose, with the thigh as a large ellipsoid at the hip and the lower leg chain running from hip down to knee for the haunch-on-ground stance.

I'm placing the haunch as a ground-sunk sphere, then working out the tail as a curving chain of points from the pelvis back and down toward the ground before rising again.

Still working out the tail tuft shape...

I'm setting up the tuft cards with a dark brown tint color, reusing the same texture for consistency. Then I'm placing the amber eyes with dark pupils, positioning them symmetrically on the skull front face near the head center.

Placing the nose as a small dark sphere near the muzzle tip, then working out the lower jaw geometry and setting up a separate 'jaw' joint parented to 'head' so the chin piece can be rigged to open and close.

I'm sorting out the joint direction conventions for the jaw hinge and confirming the head joint orientation follows the neck chain tangent. Skipping a brow ridge detail but adding a small scar capsule across the lion's left eyebrow for character.

Now I'm checking the scar's placement against the skull surface equation to make sure it sits right at the surface rather than floating outside it, adjusting the z-coordinate slightly inward. Then I'm placing the ears as scaled spheres with a tawny outer color, and starting to think through padded paw geometry and whether to add claws.

For the mane, I'm working out a ring of card elements wrapped around the head and down the neck, using a central axis and radius to position each tuft, with a second lower ring to extend coverage down toward the shoulders so the mane realistically drapes over the neck region.

For the mane paint, I'm figuring out color distance based on how far each ring item sits from a face reference point, planning blonder tones for the inner ring and darker for the outer, checking the offset distances to make sure the gradient falls naturally across the two rings.

I'm settling on a palette: a tawny brown, a deeper chocolate shade, a cream highlight, a golden blond, and a dark chocolate for shadowed areas.

For the body coat, I'm blending cream on the belly into tawny-to-deep brown on the back using a smooth transition based on vertical normal direction, so the underside softly lightens compared to the dorsal fur.

For the mane, I'm mixing blond into chocolate brown based on distance from the face, giving a gradient that darkens farther from the muzzle. I'm also checking that paint callbacks are typed correctly for position and normal vectors, and now planning the eye geometry—an amber sphere with a smaller black pupil ellipsoid scaled down on the front face.

Working out eye and pupil placement...

Defining the spine curve points...

Checking that the body position works with ends rounded by default, I'm now working out leg placement: front legs chain from the shoulder down to the ground, and the neck extends up from the chest toward the head with a narrower radius.

Tapering the neck radius to match the skull width, checking that the chest cap and neck base align at the same point, and sizing the skull sphere so the head sits around 1.13 tall. I'm estimating total model height with the mane at roughly 1.2, which feels right for a seated lion.

Now I'm plotting the front leg joints for the sphinx pose: shoulder, elbow, wrist, and toe positions pushed forward from the body, with the leg radius tapering from thick at the elbow to thinner toward the paw. I'm placing padded paw spheres at the toe tips, scaled flat and wide to look like lion paws.

For the hindquarters, I'm sketching the thigh as an ellipsoid haunch near the hip, then building out the hind leg chain of hip, knee, hock, and foot joints so the lower leg lies forward along the ground like a seated big cat, mirroring everything across left (+X) and right (-X) sides.

Thigh radius tapering from thick to thin along the leg, with an added ellipsoid mass at the hip joint to cover the thigh bulk, scaled and colored to match the coat.

Next I'm placing the hind paw as a sphere near the toe, scaled flat for a footpad shape. Then I'm working out the tail: starting it as a chain of points from the pelvis near the back of the body, curving down and back so it trails along the ground, tapering in thickness toward the tip.

Naming the tail joints as four spans plus a tip, parented to the hips joint from the spine chain. I'm tapering the tail radius down toward the tip, then adding a tuft ring of dark cards around the tail tip, oriented in the plane perpendicular to the tail's direction so they fan out radially at the end.

Joints aren't used since weights come from the ChainPoint rigid on the last span joint, with cards explicitly bound to 'tailTip'. The ring items wrap around the ChainPoint using the ring function with the line and options passed in.

For textures, I'm thinking of using tuft SVGs for both the dark tuft cards and the mane cards, maybe with two slightly different shapes (longer and wavy) picked randomly per card to add variety. The cards function takes the frame inputs, texture, and options like size, lean, bend, color, bone, vary, spin, rng, and possibly a cross parameter for extra fullness on the mane.

For the mane, I'm setting up a ring positioned slightly behind the face center so it doesn't cover the front, with cards tilted backward so they flow naturally toward the back of the head. I'm considering using two layered rings with different counts and card sizes to give the mane a shaggy, puffy look, though I need to check the radii and card lengths carefully so they don't extend too far outward from the head's outer shell.

Since the mane will likely obscure the ears anyway, I'm deciding to keep things simple by either skipping ears entirely or adding small ones tucked within the inner mane ring to avoid extra complexity.

With around 72 cards total across the mane, I'm checking that's within reasonable mesh limits. I'm also working through the body sweep setup, using a Chain as the sweep source and making sure the path resolves correctly, while double-checking how the coat color gets painted onto the surface.

Now I'm verifying joint and chain naming conventions and parent relationships across the skeleton -- spine, neck, legs, and tail chains each need valid role names and must parent correctly from the root 'body' joint through the hips and chest to the shoulders and hind legs.
